chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Al-Hasan ibn Ayoub, from Abu Aqila Al-Sayrafi, who said, 'Karram narrated to me from Abu Hamza Al-Thumali, who said,'

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Beware of leadership (al-ri'asah), and beware of treading the heels of men.' I said, 'May I be sacrificed for you! As for leadership, I have recognized it, and as for treading the heels of men, two-thirds of what is in my hand is not except from what I have treading the heels of men.' So he said to me: 'That is not where you are going with it. Beware of establishing a man besides the Proof (al-Hujjah), so you verify him in everything he says.'

key_terms.أَعْقَابَ الرِّجَالِ: Heels of men, a metaphor for following or deferring to people
key_terms.الرِّئَاسَة: Leadership or headmanship, often implying a position of authority or precedence
key_terms.الْحُجَّة: The Proof, referring to the Imam or the authoritative religious figure
key_terms.تُصَدِّقَهُ: To verify or ratify his statements

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between general deference and establishing religious authority according to this hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between the political ambition of 'seeking leadership' (al-Ri'asah) and the epistemological error of uncritical deference to any authority figure. He clarifies that true adherence requires recognizing the specific 'Proof' (al-Hujjah)—the infallible Imam—and validating his teachings, rather than merely following the footsteps of men without discernment. This highlights the Shia principle of *Tawalla* (loyalty) and *Tabarra* (disavowal) rooted in correct identification of the divine authority.
